summary: Defines a static dictionary of common SIP and SDP text for use with Signaling Compression. Because both protocols are text-based and verbose, seeding the compressor with typical strings helps shrink messages, which matters on slow links such as mobile networks.

eli5.summary: SIP messages use many repeated words. By giving the compressor a cheat sheet of common words in advance, messages shrink to much smaller size.

questions: what is the sip sdp static dictionary
how do you compress sip messages
why compress sip over slow links
subtitle: A fixed cheat sheet of common SIP and SDP text that SigComp can use to compress even the very first message.

tldr.problem: SIP and SDP are verbose text protocols built for fast links, so session setup is slow on narrow links such as radio interfaces, and compression only works well after a few messages have been exchanged.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines one static dictionary of well-known SIP and SDP strings, in a normative binary form that SigComp loads as a state item, so even the first message can be compressed against it.
tldr.outcome: The dictionary is defined once and never changes. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 4896.

today: RFC 3485 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 4896; it has not been obsoleted. The RFC itself says the dictionary is defined once and stays as is.

sections.title: Why Compress SIP and SDP
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and the Session Description Protocol (SDP) are text-based and use the UTF-8 character set. They were designed for links with plenty of bandwidth. Over narrow links, such as radio interfaces or low-speed serial links, session setup time grows substantially.

Signaling Compression (SigComp, RFC 3320) is a framework for compressing and decompressing text protocols like these. But compression only reaches its best rate after a few message exchanges, because the first message from the compressor has no stored state to compress against and is only partially compressed.

To boost compression from the first message, this memo defines a static dictionary for SIP and SDP. It constitutes a SigComp state that can be referenced in the first SIP message the compressor sends.
sections.eli5: If you and a friend always say the same long phrases, you could agree on short codes. But you need the code book before the first message, and this RFC is that code book.

sections.title: Design of the Dictionary
sections.content:
The dictionary is a collection of well-known strings that appear in most SIP and SDP messages. It is not a complete list of reserved words. It MUST be available in all SigComp implementations for SIP/SDP, and it is not meant to evolve as SIP or SDP evolve: it is defined once and stays as it is forever. That avoids the problem of upgrading and of finding out which of several versions the other end supports.

Strings are case sensitive. A header field entry includes the colon and the expected white space, and starts with the CRLF of the previous line, written [CRLF], because the CRLF that ends a header line cannot be part of the dictionary (header values vary). So messages that follow the recommended SIP formatting benefit most.

Each string has a priority from 1 to 5. A low number means a high chance of finding the string in SIP or SDP messages. Algorithms such as DEFLATE work better when the commonest strings sit at the end of the dictionary, so lower-numbered priorities are placed later.

Some entries are split to save space. For example, [CRLF]Proxy- is one entry and Authenticate: and Authorization: are separate ones. This splitting is not used for priority 1 or 2 strings. For SIP responses, each code has two entries, such as 302 and 302 Moved Temporarily, because the reason phrase is only suggested text and may be changed.
sections.eli5: The code book lists the most common phrases, and it ranks them from 1 (very common) to 5 (rare). The book never gets a new edition, so everyone always has the same one.

sections.title: The Binary Dictionary Format
sections.content:
Section 3 of the RFC gives the normative binary form, which is what a SigComp implementation includes. It was built by combining the SIP strings of Appendix A and the SDP strings of Appendix B. The result has two parts, joined to form the state value: a string subset holding every string, with overlapping substrings shared, and a table subset of pairs of length and offset. A length is stored in one byte. An offset is stored in two bytes, with 1024 added so it can be used directly if the state is loaded at address 1024.

All compression algorithms can use some or all of the string subset. Methods related to the LZ78 family can also use the table to form an initial set of tokens.

The state item is fully characterised by a few values: the state_identifier 0xfbe507dfe5e6aa5af2abb914ceaa05f99ce61ba5, a state_length of 0x12E4, a minimum_access_length of 6, and a state value shown as a hex dump. The string subset is 0x0D8C bytes and the table subset is 0x0558 bytes.
sections.eli5: The code book has two parts: a long list of phrases and an index that says where each phrase starts and how long it is.

sections.title: Using the Dictionary From SigComp
sections.content:
A SigComp program reaches the dictionary with the STATE-ACCESS instruction, using the first six bytes of the identifier (0xfbe507dfe5e6) as a partial state identifier. The RFC gives one call for the string subset and one for the table subset, each ending in the destination address in UDVM memory.

An implementation that wants to save UDVM space can load only the strings up to a chosen priority by changing the offset and length operands. The RFC lists the values for priority 1 only, 1 to 2, 1 to 3, 1 to 4 and 1 to 5. Because lower-numbered priorities sit at the end, each smaller subset is a tail of the full string subset.
sections.eli5: A device can copy the whole code book or just the most common pages, if it is short on space.

sections.title: What the Appendices Contain
sections.content: Appendix A lists the SIP input strings: URI schemes such as sip:, version strings such as SIP/2.0/UDP , method names such as INVITE, header fields, status codes with their reason phrases, and parameters. Appendix B lists the SDP strings, such as v=0[CRLF]o=, [CRLF]c=IN IP4 and [CRLF]a=rtpmap:. For each string, the tables give its priority, its offset and length in hexadecimal, and references into the specifications that motivate its inclusion. The appendices are informative; Section 3 is the normative form.
sections.eli5: The back of the book shows where each phrase came from, so you can see why it was picked.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of SigComp (RFC 3320) apply, and the memo does not introduce any known additional security risk. The IANA considerations section says "None."
sections.eli5: A fixed list of words adds no new danger, and nobody has to hand out any new numbers.
